finding.claim: The /invoice/<inv_id> route returns any invoice to any caller. It has no authentication and no check that the invoice belongs to the requester. The sibling route /my/invoice/<inv_id> does enforce `inv["customer"] != g.user["id"]`, so the omission looks like an oversight. This is a broken object-level authorization flaw (IDOR).
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP GET /invoice/<inv_id>. The attacker controls inv_id and can guess or enumerate it.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, which includes the customer field and other customer data.

trace.note: Route registered with no auth decorator and no before_request hook anywhere in the file.
INVOICES.get(inv_id) looks the record up by the attacker-supplied ID alone and does not check the owner.
The full record is returned as JSON.
For comparison, the /my/ route compares inv["customer"] with g.user["id"], but the /invoice/ route has no equivalent check.

finding.guards_checked: I looked for login_required decorators, before_request hooks, blueprint-level auth, and an ownership comparison on this route. None exist in the file, and invoices.py is the only source file in the directory. A gateway or middleware outside this repo could still enforce auth, but I found no evidence of one. Retained as a finding.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no auth decorator, before_request hook or ownership check, and returns the full record via jsonify(inv), while the sibling route at invoices.py:16 does check inv["customer"] against g.user["id"]; a gateway outside this repo could still enforce auth, but no evidence of one exists.
